title: Study that leads to deed
hookLine: his legacy joins philosophy and law
carry: study is greater because it leads to deed

cards: Two books on one shelf. One is thick with rules: how to pray, how to give, how to keep Shabbat, how a court works, what to eat.
The other is full of questions: what words about God can mean, why the commandments exist, how a mind draws near to God. The same man wrote both.
You could treat them as two different authors, the lawyer and the philosopher. But look at how each one begins and ends, and the two start to reach for each other.

teach.b: Thought and deed. First, the code starts with thought. Before a single rule about food or Shabbat, the Mishneh Torah opens with knowing that there is a first Being, and with love and awe of God.
The law book stands on a foundation of thinking.
Second, the Guide ends with deed. You heard it last week: the book of philosophy closes with Jeremiah, and with going out to do kindness, justice and righteousness. Third, an old argument.
The Talmud tells of sages gathered in an upper room in Lod, asking which is greater, study or deed. Rabbi Tarfon said deed. Rabbi Akiva said study.
And they all answered together: study is greater, because study leads to deed. Study wins by pointing past itself. Fourth, the other side of the scale.

teach.h: THE DEED IS THE MAIN THING.
teach.b: In Pirkei Avot, Shimon, the son of Rabban Gamliel, says that study isn't the main thing; the deed is. Read together, the two sayings hold each other in place.

Thought without deed goes nowhere. Deed without thought can go anywhere. That's the shape of Maimonides' legacy: the philosopher wrote law, the lawgiver wrote philosophy, and each was meant to lead into the other.

It's the shape of this week too: an argument in the margin, a rival reading, a son's prayer, an honest page, a prayer's true label, a grave by the water. Each one was a thought someone carried out into the world.

how: Jewish learning pairs study with practice: people study the laws of Shabbat, prayer or giving and then keep them, and some study Maimonides' code and his Guide side by side.

practice: Choose one idea from this week that stayed with you: credit before criticism, a second reader, saying a line slowly, an honest label, a teacher's name.
Hold it for a few breaths, then picture one small act this thought would actually do, and let the thought and the act sit together, joined.
